text.p: By Neil Winton, Science and Technology Correspondent
Communications satellites in space and television reception on Earth could be damaged by an imminent burst of solar flare activity on the sun, an expert said Friday.
Astrophysicist Piers Corbyn of long-range forecasting company Weather Action said powerful emissions of high energy particles and radiation will burst out from the sun between June 28 and July 3.
This solar action also has implications for the Earth's weather, but this won't manifest itself for a weeks and maybe months, Corbyn said.
Satellite insurance expert John Howes was sanguine about the report.

"Underwriters are aware of this potential threat to satellites, and over time they experience all kinds of solar disturbances. I can't say how right he (Corbyn) is," said Howes, deputy chairman of Lloyds insurance brokers Crawley Warren Group Plc.
"Solar storm activity goes in 11 year cycles and I'm not sure we are in a bad one at the moment," said Howes.
There are about 250 satellites in geostationary orbit 22,500 miles over the equator handling telephone and television communications.

Corbyn had forecast in April that there would be solar storm activity in May. Solar flares erupted on the sun on May 27. There were no reports of major damage to satellites. Corbyn declined to reveal details of his methods.
In April the National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) warned a solar storm was about to hit the Earth's magnetic field, with the potential to disrupt satellites and power grids.

NASA said highly charged ionised particles might strike a glancing blow at the magnetic field which protects the Earth some 100 miles (160 km) from the surface. But this solar storm turned out to be a damp squib, with the huge magnetic cloud blasted from the sun missing the Earth.
A similar storm in January may have caused the failure of a $200 million AT&T Corp communications satellite, a NASA spokesman said.
Weather Action produces weather forecasts based on the sun's activity. It has never disclosed details of its methods.

"Despite the present and recent low level of solar activity we expect at least 10 Solar flares in this period (between June 28 and July 3). These will shoot high energy particles to Earth which are likely to cause interference to communications and damage to space satellites," Corbyn told Reuters.
The impact on weather was difficult to predict.

"The deluge of ultra violet and X rays that come from the sun influence the weather but we are not sure how. The solar flares will have after-effects in coming weeks and months by speeding up and making weather fronts more active. It doesn't mean it rains everywhere, just that various fronts become more active," Corbyn said.
